reason: Re-derived the claim from scratch: the graph does contain the 4 Dependency rows with literal `${...}` property strings instead of substituted versions, confirming the analyst's raw observation. But the claim that "the actual pinned version used at build time cannot be verified from this scan" is false — the real pinned versions are trivially available in the same source tree, one file away from where the CPG extracted the dependency declarations. The project root pom.xml (org.eclipse.parsson:project, the actual reactor root — not an external/unknown parent) declares all four properties as concrete literals: jakarta.json-api.version=2.1.2, jakarta.annotation-api.version=2.1.1, jakarta.xml.bind-api.version=4.0.0, jakarta.ws.rs-api.version=3.1.0. These are not inherited from an opaque external BOM and are not overridable by unknown CI variables — they are fixed constants in the repo. Standard Maven property substitution resolves every child-module `<version>${jakarta.*.version}</version>` to these exact values at build time, deterministically. This is not a supply-chain visibility gap in the scanned application; it is a limitation of the CPG/Dependency extraction step (it captured the literal XML text of the `<version>` element without performing Maven property interpolation), which I was able to resolve myself in under a minute by reading the parent pom.xml. There is no missing information, no outdated/unverifiable component, and no actionable remediation beyond "read the one-hop-away properties block" — which I just did. CWE-1104 (unmaintained component) also does not fit since there is no evidence of staleness; the versions found (jakarta.json-api 2.1.2, jakarta.ws.rs-api 3.1.0, jakarta.xml.bind-api 4.0.0, jakarta.annotation-api 2.1.1) are all recent Jakarta EE 10-era releases. This is a scanner artifact, not a genuine security finding.

reason: The graph fact is accurate (jaxb-impl:3.0.1 is a declared Dependency), but re-deriving the security claim from source shows there is no XXE/deserialization attack surface attached to this dependency in this codebase. This repo is eclipse-ee4j/parsson (a JSON-Processing implementation); jaxb-impl is NOT used by the core library at all -- it is scoped `runtime` only in the optional `demos/twitter` demo module (root pom.xml:458-462 pins it to 3.0.1 inside the 'all' profile; demos/twitter/pom.xml:49-53 consumes it). A repo-wide grep for JAXBContext/Unmarshaller/.unmarshal(/createUnmarshaller found zero matches anywhere in the tree. The only call touching a jakarta.xml.bind class anywhere in the codebase is `DatatypeConverter.printBase64Binary(res)` in demos/twitter/src/main/java/org/eclipse/parsson/demos/twitter/TwitterObjectSearch.java:120 (confirmed via graph: CpgCall method_full_name 'jakarta.xml.bind.DatatypeConverter.printBase64Binary', file_path demos/twitter/.../TwitterObjectSearch.java, line 120), which base64-encodes a locally-computed HMAC-SHA1 signature byte array for a Twitter OAuth header -- it never parses, unmarshals, or binds any XML, let alone attacker-controlled XML. There is no JAXB unmarshalling/binding code path for jaxb-impl to exercise, so the 'worth checking NVD for XXE/deserialization CVEs' framing has no corresponding vulnerable usage pattern in this codebase. Additionally this demo is an offline CLI tool requiring locally-stored hardcoded Twitter API credentials (twitterconfig.properties) -- not a network-reachable attacker-facing entry point. exploit_search returned 'corpus unavailable: not indexed', so no exploit-reference grounding was possible, but that is moot given the absence of any exploitable code path. Per the rules, since the vulnerable structure the lead implies (an exploitable XML-binding/deserialization surface) is not actually present in the source, this is rejected rather than left inconclusive.
